String Methods

The one idea to landA slice and a string method both hand you back a new string and leave the original exactly as it was — so you keep only what you assign. And strip works from the two ends inwards, one character at a time, stopping the moment it meets a character you did not name.

Recap · For Loop

Quick Check

What is the last thing this prints?

word = "NIAT"
for each_char in word:
    print(each_char)
  • NIAT
  • T
  • N
  • nothing — word is not a sequence

2 — T. The loop takes the characters one at a time, in order, and prints four separate lines. The last character is the last line.NIAT <- lastFour lines, not one. A string is a sequence of characters.

And the last number here?

for number in range(3, 7):
    print(number)
  • 7
  • 6
  • 3
  • 4

2 — 6. It starts at 3 and stops before 7. Four numbers: 3, 4, 5, 6.3456 <- last7 never reachedThe end value is where it stops, not the last value it uses. Today’s slices do exactly the same thing.

Last session’s challenge. What does this print?

a = "Python"
b = ""
for i in range(1, len(a)):
    b = b + "-" + a[i]
print(b)
  • P-y-t-h-o-n
  • -y-t-h-o-n
  • Python
  • y-t-h-o-n

2 — -y-t-h-o-n. The loop starts at index 1, so P is never added — and the first thing it adds is a hyphen. b = a[0] fixes both.a[0] P never usedi = 1 b = "-y"printed: -y-t-h-o-n

String Methods · Isdigit

Type It, Then Break It

Type this and run it. Then try "984a" and "12345" on line 1.

pin = "4748"
is_digit = pin.isdigit()
is_4_digit = (len(pin) == 4)
is_valid = is_digit and is_4_digit
print(is_valid)

Mine is the voucher from the start of the session. I copied it off the slip, so line 1 on my screen is this:

pin = "4748 "

Put that on your line 1 — the space goes inside the quotes, at the end. Run it.

Same four digits. Same order.

Add one line and run it again. Which of the two went False?

print(is_digit, is_4_digit)

Then say what the fifth character is. It is on your screen, and you cannot see it.

Instructor guide

Session 15 · String Methods · 75 minutes · read this once before class, keep it open on your laptop during

How to use this

One entry per slide, in the order you will present them. How it goes is the thread of the slide — what to say, in order. Quoted phrases are worth saying close to as written; the rest is yours, in your own words.

Nothing starts out of nowhere. Every slide begins from something the room already has — a voucher they have read, the program still on their screens, the answer somebody just gave — and ends by handing over to the next slide. If you find yourself opening a slide cold, go back one step and connect it.

Three habits carry the session. Walk it in small steps and check as you go — “so if the space is still there, is it four characters or five? Five, right?” Ask before you tell, always. And offer doubts often: “any doubts here?” costs four seconds and saves ten minutes.

One sentence is the whole session. A slice and a method both hand back a new string and leave the original alone, so you keep only what you assign. Say it at the walker, say it again at the trace, and the exit poll will tell you whether it landed.

Slide by slide

Opening · 1 min · slide 1 of 30

Welcome

How it goes
  1. Greet them and take attendance while this is up.
  2. Nothing about the topic yet, and no worksheets yet — they come out at the first activity.
  • Attendance only. Keep it to a minute.

Watch for stragglers at the back. Settle the room before the title slide.

Opening · slide 2 of 30

Title — String Methods

How it goes
  1. Name the topic: “today it is string methods — and one more way of slicing a string.”
  2. Make the promise early, before they are holding anything: “you will get a worksheet part-way through, and every sheet you write on today gets collected at the end.”
  3. Do not define anything yet — connect backwards instead: “but first, what stayed from last session?”
  • Read the title and move. Retrieval before new material.

Watch for the urge to list the seven methods here. The list arrives at slide 15, after they have needed two of them.

Warm-up poll · slide 3 of 30

Recap — the title slide

How it goes
  1. “Three quick questions on last session. Nothing new in them.”
  2. Set the rule before the first question so nobody is surprised: “pick your answer in your head, do not shout it out.”
  • Five seconds on this slide. It is a signpost.

Watch for nothing here. Move on.

Warm-up poll · 4 min · slide 4 of 30 · three questions

Recap poll — three from For Loop

How it goes
  1. Read the question and the four options aloud. Let the timer run — that is their thinking time.
  2. Count the room option by option: “how many say option one? Hands up.” … two … three … four. Say each count out loud: “okay, about twenty for option two.”
  3. Only now reveal. Then explain briefly — a line for every option, from the table below, wrong ones included.
  4. Same three moves for Q2 and Q3.
  5. Q2 is the one to linger on for ten seconds: “the end value is where it stops, not the last one it uses. Hold on to that — today’s slices do exactly the same thing.”
  6. Hand off after Q3: “good. Now the new thing — and we are starting with something you can already do.”
  • Count before you reveal. Once they know the answer you cannot see what they thought.
  • These three timers start by themselves. The rest of the session’s timers do not.
QOptSay after the reveal
Q11That would be printing the whole word once. The loop prints four separate lines.
2 ✓Correct. The characters come out one at a time, in order, so the last one is last.
3N is the first line, not the last.
4A string is a sequence of characters. That is exactly why this works.
Q217 is where it stops. It is never used.
2 ✓Correct. 3, 4, 5, 6 — four numbers, and it stops before 7.
33 is the first one printed.
44 is how many numbers there are, not the last one.
Q31That is the corrected version, from b = a[0]. This one starts from an empty string.
2 ✓Correct. The loop starts at index 1, so P is never added — and the first thing added is a hyphen.
3Every pass adds a hyphen. There is no way back to plain Python.
4Close — but the very first thing the loop adds is the hyphen, before the y.

Watch for the count on Q2. If more than about a third pick option 1, slow down on the end index at slide 10 — it is the same rule and they will meet it again in the exit poll.

Hook · 3 min · slide 5 of 30 · three presses

The voucher that prints your PIN with dashes in it

How it goes
  1. Start from something everyone in the room has done: “the Wi-Fi voucher, the coupon slip, the card on the back of a recharge — they never print the number plain. They print it in bits.”
  2. Put the question to them and wait: “read it out. What do you type into the Wi-Fi box?” Take it from the room. They will say four seven four eight without a pause.
  3. Do not praise it yet — make it strange: “there are seven characters on that voucher. You typed four. Where did the other three go?”
  4. Press once. The dashes get boxed and the index row appears. “Your eye threw these three away. The program does not get to do that — it gets all seven.”
  5. Press again. Say nothing while the dashes collapse, then: “that is what you did in half a second. Now we have to write down how you did it.”
  6. Offer doubts, then hand off: “any doubts? Good — now you tell me where else something arrives with junk printed inside it.”
  • Three presses, in order. The button tells you what the next one does.
  • r replays it from the start if you want to run it twice.

Watch for somebody answering “4-7-4-8” with the dashes. That is the right answer to a different question — ask them what they would actually type.

Your turn · 1 min · slide 6 of 30

Your turn — where else does junk arrive inside the thing you want?

How it goes
  1. Ask it exactly as it is on the slide, then count ten in your head. Do not fill the silence.
  2. Take two or three out loud. A card number printed in fours, a date with slashes, a roll number with a slash in it, an OTP typed with spaces, a phone number with a space after the code.
  3. Close it by naming what all of theirs have in common: “in every one of those, the thing you want is inside a longer string. So — how do we get a part of a string out?”
  • No worksheets yet. They come out two slides from now.
  • Do not write the examples on the board. Say them back and move.

Watch for a room that offers nothing. Narrow it: “anyone had to type a card number today?” One example is enough to move on.

Agenda · 1 min · slide 7 of 30

Agenda — String Slicing to String Methods

How it goes
  1. Two halves, and say which is which: “first, slicing with a step — that is the voucher. Then a set of ready-made tools Python gives you for strings.”
  2. Hand off to the first half: “and slicing, you already know half of.”
  • Thirty seconds. Do not read the boxes out one by one.

Watch for nothing. This is a signpost.

Slicing · 5 min · slide 8 of 30

Slicing — a part of a string, from one index up to another

How it goes
  1. Open from what they have: “this one you have already done. message holds Hi Ravi, and we want just the name.”
  2. Point at the index row and ask, do not tell: “which index does R sit on?” Take it from the room. Three.
  3. Then the end: “the name ends at index 6. So why does it say 7?” Wait. Somebody will connect it to the poll: it stops before the end index.
  4. Say the shape once, plainly: “start index, colon, end index. It gives you a new string — message is untouched.”
  5. Offer doubts, then hand off: “any doubts? Now here is one this cannot do.”
  • Board: write message[3:7] and leave it up. The next slide is compared against it.

Watch for “3 to 7 is five characters”. Count the highlighted boxes on the slide with them: 3, 4, 5, 6 — four.

Slicing · slide 9 of 30

Accessing parts of a string — can we get “Ravi” out of this one?

How it goes
  1. Connect it to the hook by name: “this is the voucher again, with letters instead of digits.”
  2. Ask the question on the slide and let them try it with what they have: “we know start colon end. Give me the slice that pulls Ravi out of this.” Thirty seconds, no worksheet, just out loud.
  3. Take one answer and run it on the board, honestly: secret_message[1:8] gives R-a-v-i. “Close. What is still in there that we do not want?”
  4. Name the gap rather than the solution: “every tool we have takes a run of characters. We want every second one. That is the thing we are missing.”
  • Do not say the word step yet. It arrives on the next slide as the answer to this.

Watch for a student who already knows the third number. Do not shut it down — “hold that, you are one slide ahead” — and ask them for the two numbers before it.

The step · 6 min · slide 10 of 30

Extended slicing — the third number

How it goes
  1. Answer the gap you just named: “so Python gives us a third number, and it is called the step.”
  2. Say what it does in their words, not a definition: “how far you jump to get the next character.”
  3. Walk the arithmetic on the slide out loud, one jump at a time, asking each one: “we start at 1. Add the step — where do we land?” 3. “And again?” 5. “And again?” 7.
  4. Now the end index, because it is the half they get wrong: “we are at 7. Add 2 — that is 9. Do we take it?” No — 8 is the end, and it stops before the end.
  5. Offer doubts here specifically: “any doubts about the third number? This is the whole first half of the session.”
  • Board, and leave it up all session: variable[start : end : step].

Watch for the assumption that step 2 means “two characters at a time”. It means skip to the index two further on — one character is kept, not two.

The step · slide 11 of 30

secret_message[1:8:2] — the whole thing, end to end

How it goes
  1. This is the same string they just failed to cut, now with the answer on it: “same message, same problem, one more number.”
  2. Read the jumps off the slide in one pass — 1, 3, 5, 7 — and then the result: Ravi.
  3. Ask the one that matters: “index 8 is the last dash. Why is it not in the answer?” Wait. Two answers are correct here — the jump lands past it, and 8 is the end index anyway.
  4. Hand off to the paper: “right — worksheets are coming out, and you are going to mark exactly where this thing lands.”
  • Do not move on until somebody has said “it stops before 8” out loud.

Watch for heads nodding at the picture. The picture is easy; producing it is not, which is what the next four minutes are for.

Pen & paper · 4 min · slide 12 of 30 · worksheet page 1, task 1

Mark every landing

How it goes
  1. Hand the worksheets out now — this is the only hand-out moment in the session. Remind them as they go round: “name and roll number at the top. These come back to me at the end.”
  2. Give the instruction off the slide and be exact about the place: “in the number row, underneath the string. Circle every index it lands on. Box every index it does not.”
  3. Start the timer yourself and let them work. Two minutes.
  4. Walk the rows. Keep talking as you go, one line at a time, not all at once: “are you guys done?” · “any doubts about the task? Ask now.” · “one minute left.”
  5. Pens down first, then press Next and say the check. Not before: “each circle should be two further along than the one before it. And index 8 should be boxed, not circled.”
  6. Then the answer, from them: “so which four did you circle?” 1, 3, 5, 7. “And the string it gives?” "Ravi".
  • Press play on the timer. It does not start by itself.
  • Do not correct individuals while walking. Note what you see and say it to the whole room afterwards.

Watch for sheets with 0, 2, 4, 6 circled — that is the hook’s voucher, which started at index 0. Say so out loud: “that is the right method on the wrong start index.” Answers: circled 1, 3, 5, 7 · boxed 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 · the string is "Ravi".

Hands-on 1 · 5 min · slide 13 of 30 · worksheet page 1, task 2

Predict three, then run them

How it goes
  1. Set the rule before they touch anything: “all three written down first. The laptop is how you find out whether you were right, not how you find the answer.”
  2. Timer, two and a half minutes, while they fill the middle column. Walk the rows: “come on, let us see who has all three” · “thirty seconds, finish the last row.”
  3. Press Next. Now they type it and fill the last column. “Tick the ones you got right. Circle the wrong ones and write the real answer beside them — do not rub anything out.”
  4. Take a show of hands on the second one only: “how many had Wrl?” It is the one with the gap of four.
  5. Press Next for the last row and ask it straight: “three slices came out of a. Print a again — what is left in it?” Wait for the answer. All nine characters. Nothing was taken out of it.
  6. Hand off: “hold on to that. Now watch what the slice actually does.”
  • Two timers on this card, one per step. Both are started by you.
  • Nine lines with fifty-five first-years is three minutes, not one. Do not claw it back from the prediction step.

Watch for anyone typing during the first step. Answers: a[1:6:3] → ar · a[0:9:4] → Wrl · a[2:9:3] → tfl · a → Waterfall, unchanged.

Follow the step · 3 min · slide 14 of 30

Follow the step — the slice, running

How it goes
  1. The slider is already on 3 — a step nobody has worked out yet. Say the program out loud, then: “write down what this prints. Everybody, on your sheet margin, now.”
  2. Take the split before you press anything: “hands up for two characters. Three characters. More than three.” Do not say who is right.
  3. Press Play. Say nothing while the dot walks.
  4. Then point at the grey: “look at what it never touched. Those characters are not in name — and they are still in secret. Both rows are on the screen at once.”
  5. Now drag the slider to 2 and use One step, one press at a time, so the room calls each landing before it happens: 1, 3, 5, 7.
  6. Hand off: “that is slicing finished. The rest of the session is a set of ready-made tools — and they all behave like this one.”
  • One step is the control to use when the room disagrees. r resets it.
  • Budget three minutes. It is a reveal, not a lesson.

Watch for the answer at step 3: R-i, three characters including a dash. If the room expected Ra they are adding 1, not the step.

Methods · 2 min · slide 15 of 30

String methods — the toolbox

How it goes
  1. Frame it as saved work, not new syntax: “checking whether every character is a digit — you could write a loop for that. Python has already written it.”
  2. Read the seven names once, no explanations. “We use all of these today.”
  3. Say the shape, and write it on the board: the_string.method() — “the string first, then a dot, then the name, then brackets.”
  4. Hand off to the first one with a problem, not a definition: “start with a PIN.”
  • Board: str_var.method(). It stays up for the rest of the session.
  • Two minutes. Do not explain seven methods on one slide.

Watch for pens copying all seven names down. Tell them not to — the map at the end has them sorted by what they give back.

isdigit · 4 min · slide 16 of 30

Scenario — is the PIN the user typed a valid one?

How it goes
  1. Open from their own phone: “the four-digit PIN on your UPI app. Before it accepts one, it has to check two things.”
  2. Ask for them rather than reading them: “what would you check?” Wait. You want all digits and exactly four.
  3. Take a wrong-but-reasonable answer seriously if it comes — “not the same digit four times” is a real rule, just not today’s.
  4. Then the one they would have to write themselves: “how would you check that every character is a digit, with what you know?” A loop over the characters. “Right — and that is the loop Python has already written for you.”
  • Do not read the two bullets off the slide. Get them from the room first, then point at the slide.

Watch for the room jumping to len only. Length is half the check; the other half is what isdigit is for.

isdigit · slide 17 of 30

Isdigit — True only if every character is a digit

How it goes
  1. Read the shape off the slide: “the string, dot, isdigit, brackets. Nothing goes in the brackets.”
  2. Be precise about what comes back, because it is the thing they confuse: “this one does not give you a string. It gives you True or False.”
  3. Ask before revealing: “4748 — True or False?” Then a harder one: “984a?” Then the one that catches them: “how about 47.8?” False — a full stop is not a digit.
  4. Hand off to the keyboard: “type it and try a few of your own.”
  • Board, under the shape: isdigit → True / False. You will add to this list twice more.

Watch for “it checks if it is a number”. Every character, and only digits — no minus sign, no full stop, no space.

Hands-on 2 · 5 min · slide 18 of 30 · three steps

Type it, then break it

How it goes
  1. Step one: they type the five lines and run them. True. Then "984a" and "12345" on line 1 — False both times, for two different reasons. Ask which reason each time.
  2. Walk the rows while they work: “are you guys getting True?” · “any doubts on line 3? Ask now.”
  3. Step two, and this is the beat — frame it as your own copy-paste, not as a test, and do not warn them: “mine came off the voucher, so my line 1 has a space after the digits, inside the quotes. Put that in and run it.”
  4. Let them react before you say anything. It goes False, and nothing on screen looks different.
  5. Step three: add the extra print and ask which half failed. Both did — isdigit is False because a space is not a digit, and the length is 5, not 4.
  6. Hand off with the problem, not the fix: “so a character you cannot see broke it. And you will not always be the one who typed it.”
  • Say “inside the quotes, at the end” twice. Half the room will put the space outside.
  • Timer on step one only. Steps two and three run on your voice.

Watch for the student who deletes the space to “fix” it. Ask them what they would do if a user typed it. Answers: "4748 " → isdigit False, len 5.

strip · 7 min · slide 19 of 30

The same number, twice — and Python says False

How it goes
  1. Connect it straight to what just broke: “same invisible character, now in a place you did not type.”
  2. Read the two numbers off the slide, digit for digit, and ask before showing the output: “same or not same?” Hands up for same.
  3. Only then point at False. Let it sit for a second.
  4. Ask for the reason rather than giving it: “every digit matches. So why?” Wait. Somebody says the spaces.
  5. Make it about them, not the slide: “you have done this — pasted a mobile number with a space on the end into a form, and it said no such account.”
  6. Hand off: “so we need a way to take those off. Python has one.”
  • Board: " 9876543210 " != "9876543210". Leave it up for the next two slides.

Watch for “the computer is wrong”. It is not — a space is a character like any other, and the two strings are genuinely different.

strip · slide 20 of 30

Strip — takes the spaces off both ends

How it goes
  1. Give it as the answer to the slide before: “strip. Empty brackets means spaces.”
  2. Read line 2 off the slide and stop on the left half of it: “mobile = mobile.strip(). Why is mobile = there at all?” Wait. Take whatever comes.
  3. Answer it in one sentence and mean it: “because strip does not change the string. It makes a new one and hands it back. If nobody catches it, it is gone.”
  4. Point back at the walker if it helps: “same as the slice — secret was still all nine characters.”
  5. Offer doubts here. This is the sentence the whole session turns on.
  • Board, next to the isdigit line: strip → a new string.

Watch for nodding. They will nod at this and still write the bare call twenty minutes from now — which is exactly what the trace on page 2 is for.

strip · slide 21 of 30

Strip with characters — and the dot in the middle survives

How it goes
  1. Extend it, do not restate it: “spaces are the default. You can also name the characters you want gone.”
  2. Read the input out exactly — M.Ravi. — and ask before the output: “we strip full stops. How many dots come off?” Hands up for two, hands up for one.
  3. Reveal, and name the rule in their words: “one. It works from the two ends inwards and stops the moment it meets something that is not a full stop.”
  4. Walk it once, out loud, from the left: “M is not a dot — it stops immediately. From the right: dot, gone; i is not a dot, stop.”
  5. Add the second half plainly: “and what you put in the brackets is a set of characters, not a word. strip(" ,.") takes off spaces, commas and dots, in any order.”
  6. Hand off to the worksheet: “right. Page 2, and there is a program that does not do what it looks like it does.”
  • Say “from the ends inwards” at least twice. It is the exit poll.

Watch for “it removes all the dots”. Ask them what the output on the slide would be if it did — MRavi, and it is not.

Activity · 8 min · slide 22 of 30 · worksheet page 2, task 3

Trace it, then run it

How it goes
  1. Set the task without saying what the program is for: “five lines. One row each. After every line, write what name holds — in full, with the quotes.” Do not say it cleans up a name.
  2. Fill row 1 together, out loud, and say what the machine does before what the line means: “line 1 puts this string into name — two spaces, M dot Ravi dot, two spaces. Write it with the spaces showing.”
  3. Timer, four minutes, for rows 2 to 5. Walk the rows. Keep talking: “are you guys on row 3?” · “any doubts about what row 3 is asking? Ask now.” · “two minutes left.”
  4. Pens down, then say the check — not before: “your row for line 3 should say exactly the same thing as your row for line 2.” Let that land.
  5. Take the reason from the room: “line 3 has no name = on it. It builds the new string and throws it away.”
  6. Press Next: they type it and run it. It prints M.RAVI. — with the dot still on the end.
  7. Press Next for the fix: line 3 becomes name = name.strip("."). Run it: M.RAVI. Ask why the first dot is still there. Because it is not at an end.
  • Press play on the timer. Four minutes on the trace, then move whatever the room has.
  • Do not reveal the answers row by row on the board — the check in step 4 is what finds the divergence.

Watch for a row 3 that says "M.Ravi" — that is the whole point of the task, and it is the most common answer in the room. Answers: 1 "  M.Ravi.  " · 2 "M.Ravi." · 3 "M.Ravi." unchanged · 4 "M.RAVI." · 5 prints M.RAVI. · fixed, it prints M.RAVI.

replace · 5 min · slide 23 of 30

Replace — every occurrence, not just the first

How it goes
  1. Open from a thing they have done: “you have typed the same word wrong all the way through an assignment. What do you press?” Ctrl+H. “Python has that too.”
  2. Read the shape: “the old part first, then the new part.”
  3. Ask before revealing: “there are two tehs in that sentence. How many get fixed?” Wait. Both.
  4. Then the question that matters, and point at the board: “does the sentence change, or do we get a new one?” A new one — which is why line 2 starts with sentence = again.
  5. Hand off: “that is three of them that hand back a string. Here is one that does not.”
  • Board: replace → a new string, under strip.

Watch for “it changes the sentence”. Ask what print(sentence) would show if line 2 were left off.

replace · slide 24 of 30

Startswith — True or False, not a new string

How it goes
  1. Open from the padlock: “the little lock in the address bar. How does the browser decide to show it?”
  2. Read the shape, then ask: “what comes back from this one — a string, or True or False?” Wait. They have seen this once already with isdigit.
  3. Be exact about the argument: “it checks the whole thing you give it, in order, right at the front.”
  4. One quick test off the slide: “would http:// pass this check?” No — and that is the point of it.
  5. Hand off to them writing one: “there is a matching one for the other end. Nobody is going to show you it.”
  • Board: startswith → True / False.

Watch for confusion with in. startswith is about the front only, not anywhere in the string.

You write endswith · slide 25 of 30

You write this one

How it goes
  1. Give the spec and nothing else: “print True if it is a Gmail address, False if it is not. There is no code on the screen to copy.”
  2. Timer, two minutes. Walk the rows: “anyone got it in two lines?” · “what are you checking — the front or the back?”
  3. Take the method name from the room, not from you. Somebody will try endswith because it is the obvious mirror. That is the transfer, and it is the point of the beat.
  4. Press Next. Hands up for True then False. Then the sorting question: “what did it hand back — a string, or an answer?”
  5. Close the set out loud, pointing at the board: “four give a string, three give True or False. That is the whole list.”
  • Press play on the timer.
  • If the room is stuck after a minute, narrow it: “you have used the one for the front. What would the one for the back be called?”

Watch for endswith("gmail.com") without the @. It is True for ravi@notgmail.com too — worth saying out loud if you see it.

upper · 3 min · slide 26 of 30

Upper, and lower is its mirror

How it goes
  1. Open from a form they have filled: “NAME IN BLOCK LETTERS. The form does not trust you to do it, so the program does it.”
  2. Read the shape and ask the now-familiar question: “string or True/False?” A string.
  3. Ask about a mixed one before showing it: “AyUsH — what comes out?” All capitals, whatever went in.
  4. Give them lower in one line and make them run it: “there is a mirror of this. Change upper to lower on your screen and run it — thirty seconds.”
  5. Hand off: “that is all seven. Let us put them in one picture.”
  • Board, last two entries: upper, lower → a new string.
  • Thirty seconds on the keyboard, no timer. Keep it moving.

Watch for a student saying the original is now capitals. It is not, unless they assigned it — same rule as every other method today.

Key takeaways · 3 min · slide 27 of 30 · seven presses

Key takeaways — the session as one map

How it goes
  1. Before the first press, ask for it in one sentence: “one sentence — what was today about? Write it in the margin of your sheet.” Thirty seconds.
  2. Take two out loud. Contrast a vague one with a precise one without naming anyone: “‘string methods’ is the topic. ‘They give you a new string’ is the idea.”
  3. Now press through the map, one box at a time, and let the room say each one before it appears.
  4. Stop on the last two and say them as they are written. The red one is the one that costs marks.
  5. Hand off: “one question before you go, and it is a hard one.”
  • Seven presses. Reveal next, or the right arrow key.

Watch for summaries that list the seven names. Push once for what is true of all of them.

Exit poll · 3 min · slide 28 of 30 · hard floor

Exit poll — one question

How it goes
  1. This runs however far behind you are. If you have four minutes left, this is what they are for.
  2. Read the story and the four inputs out loud, exactly as written. Do not paraphrase the values — the spaces are the question.
  3. Start the timer. Two and a half minutes, silent. Nobody answers out loud.
  4. Count all four options before revealing: “hands up for one … two … three … four.” Say the counts out loud.
  5. Reveal, then give a line for every option from the table — especially the wrong ones, because each one is a different mistake.
  6. Close: “if you picked a wrong one, you know exactly which half of today to read again tonight.”
  • Press play on the timer. It does not start by itself.
  • Do not let anyone shout the answer. The value of this one is the count.
OptSay after the reveal
1 04748Picked by anyone who thinks strip only ever removes spaces. It removes whatever you name — here the leading zero goes, leaving four digits, and it prints.
2  4748 Picked by anyone reading " 0" as the two-character word “space-zero”. It is a set: a space or a zero, either one. Both spaces come off, and it prints.
3 47480Picked by anyone who thinks it works from the left only. It works from both ends — the trailing zero goes too, and it prints.
4 4 748 ✓Correct. The space is in the middle, so strip never reaches it, and isdigit is False because a space is not a digit. Lines 4 and 5 are never reached — nothing at all is printed.

Watch for a big count on option 2. That is the “strip takes a word” misreading, and it is worth two minutes at the start of next session.

Close · 1 min · slide 29 of 30

Feedback

How it goes
  1. “Fill this in before you leave — it is thirty seconds.”
  2. While they do, say what practice to go and do: the coding questions on the portal, today’s methods.
  • Do not start a new explanation here, however good the question is. Take it after class.

Watch for the room packing up during this. Say the sheet line before they stand.

Close · slide 30 of 30

Thank You

How it goes
  1. Close the loop you opened in minute one: “sheets to the front as you leave — name and roll number on top.”
  2. “See you next session.”
  • Collect every sheet. You promised at the start; finish it.

Watch for sheets left on desks. Count them against attendance before you leave the room.

Common guidelines

Never start a slide cold

Every slide should open from something the room already has — a voucher they just read, the program still on their screens, the answer somebody just gave — and close by pointing at the next one. If a slide ever feels abrupt, the fix is almost always one sentence at the end of the previous slide, not a longer explanation on this one.

Walk it in steps, and check as you go

Do not deliver a finished explanation. Say one step, then ask the next one as a question: “so if the space is still on the end, is that four characters or five? Five, right? Good.” The “right?” is not filler — it is a checkpoint, and if the room does not answer it, you have found the gap before it cost you anything. Offer doubts at the end of every concept slide: four seconds, and it saves ten minutes later.

How every poll runs

Same three moves each time. Let them think — the timer is thinking time, not pressure. Count all four options out loud before you reveal anything; once they know the answer you can no longer see what they actually thought. Then reveal and say a line about every option, wrong ones included — a wrong option nobody explains is a wrong option they keep.

Picking students — the rotation rule

Never call a name. Call a group, so nobody is singled out and nobody can hide: roll numbers ending 1, 2 or 3 · first names starting with a vowel · the window row · everyone whose sheet has all three rows of task 2 filled. Different group every question, different sets next session. If the same four hands answer everything, you have a quiet class and a loud four, not an engaged class.

When nobody answers

Count ten seconds in your head before you fill the silence. It almost never takes ten. If it does, narrow the question — “is it two characters or three?” — rather than answering it yourself.

Why paper before the keyboard

Typing is fast and forgiving: a wrong guess costs nothing, because the machine answers in half a second. On paper there is no machine to ask, so the only way to fill the row is to run the program in your own head — which is the skill the whole session is building. The keyboard afterwards is not the exercise; it is the marking scheme. Skip the paper step and the room still gets the right answers, just from the interpreter rather than from themselves.

Say it the same way every time

Two phrases in this session mean something precise, and a loose version of either will cost you the exit poll.

  • “It gives you a new string” — never “it changes the string”. Nothing today changes a string. If a student says “it changes it”, ask them what print would show if the assignment were left off.
  • “From the two ends inwards” — never just “it removes the dots”. strip stops at the first character you did not name, and everything past that point stays.
  • “The step is how far you jump” — not “how many you take”. One character is kept per jump.

Reading the room

  • Fewer than half the hands up on a poll — they did not understand the question, not the topic. Read the question again; do not explain the answer.
  • The same four voices every time — rotation rule, immediately.
  • Heads down and no typing during a hands-on — the instruction was unclear, not the task. Say it again in one sentence.
  • Nobody asks a doubt when you offer — walk the rows instead. The doubts come one to one, not to the whole room.
  • They finish the trace in under two minutes — they guessed. Ask one of them to read row 3 aloud.

Spaces on the worksheet

Task 3 asks for strings written “with the spaces showing”. Some students will write "__M.Ravi.__", some will draw boxes, some will leave gaps. All three are correct. What is not correct is writing M.Ravi. with no quotes at all — then nobody, including them, can tell how many spaces they meant. Say that when you hand the sheet out.

If you are running behind

The order to give things up in, worst case first. Slide 26, upper and lower — one sentence and a thirty-second edit, and the map still carries it. Slide 25, writing endswith — say it out loud instead of having them write it. The third step of the trace on slide 22 — the fix to line 3 can be set as homework. Never give up the exit poll, and never give up the pens-down check on slide 22: those two are the session.
